understanding.purpose: An issue tracker for quick triage: identify each issue, read its title, compare severity/status, and see who owns it and how recently it changed.
understanding.reading: Readers scan left to right: ID anchors the row, Title carries the main meaning, Severity and Status support triage, Assignee and Updated form a right-side ownership/recency rail. Statuses and severities are compared vertically; titles are read as sentences.
groups: ID + Title — row identity and description; Title should dominate the reading path
Severity + Status — triage state; short categorical values compared together
Assignee + Updated — ownership and recency; related right-hand metadata
keep_intact: Assignee handles such as m.garcia and a.okafor
Status labels as semantic units where possible
may_wrap: Title between words; row height can absorb two or three title lines
Status between words only in compressed metadata designs, never inside a word

preferred.name: r0A
preferred.note: Protect every metadata value on one line and give all remaining width to Title, which wraps to two lines where needed.

bad.name: r0B
bad.note: Maximize Title width while compressing Status and Updated just enough to wrap at word boundaries, keeping all identifiers and single words unbroken.
bad.why: Status is squeezed to 82px so 'In progress' breaks onto two lines, and Updated at 83px splits every ISO date after the first hyphen ('2024-' / '06-02'), damaging scanability and forcing all rows to 60px.

bad.name: r0C
bad.note: Metadata-forward layout: give Status and Updated generous single-line space and let Title wrap more aggressively for readers who scan state and recency first.
bad.why: Title is under-allocated at 206px, forcing the longest title to three lines, while Status (112px) and especially Updated (138px) carry large dead space; the result is uneven row heights and a bloated, poorly proportioned table.

rationale: The table is scanned first by ID, then by title, with severity, assignee, status, and updated acting as short categorical attributes. r0A gives Title the flexible remainder while keeping every short field at its one-line width, so only titles wrap and only to two lines. r0B breaks status and dates, and r0C overfeeds the right-hand columns while starving Title. The compact, even two-line rhythm of r0A is the best reading experience.

general: Allocate width by scanning role: identifiers and categorical fields need just enough for one line; free-text fields absorb the flexible remainder.
Keep dates, status labels, and other short comparison values unbroken; hyphen-splitting dates is worse than wrapping a title.
A compact table with consistent one- or two-line rows usually beats a taller table with concentrated dead space.
specific: Here Title is the only genuinely long free-text column, so it should receive most of the slack; Severity, Assignee, Status, and Updated are short categorical fields.
The longest title needs roughly 245px of column width to stay at two lines; at 206px it becomes three lines.
Updated needs about 108px for one-line ISO dates, and Status needs about 98px for 'In progress'.

tradeoffs: A designer could give Title more width (as r0B does) to reduce title wrapping, but only by squeezing Status and Updated into broken lines; that trade is not worth it. Conversely, r0C protects the short fields but wastes width on them and creates a three-line title row.
uncertain: The exact Title threshold between two and three lines is font- and word-break-dependent, and some designers might treat r0C as merely suboptimal rather than bad because its data remains intact.

critique.good: Every metadata column sits exactly at its natural single-line width: ID 96 holds BUG-2041 (75), Severity 80 holds Critical/High/Low (59), Assignee 87 holds m.garcia/a.okafor (66), Status 98 holds “In progress” (77), Updated 108 holds 2024-06-02 (87). Nothing is split mid-token, dates and statuses stack into clean vertical runs, and the title never needs more than two lines. It is the only layout that achieves all of this.
critique.problems: Title gets only 250px (35% of the table) and 4 of 6 titles break into a short, weak second line (“on Safari 17”, “containing emoji”, “notification worker”); row heights alternate 36/60, so the left edge of the table pulses rather than flows. The date column sits flush against the right border with only its 21px padding.
critique.cause: The five metadata columns consume 469px (65%) at their exact minimum one-line widths (96+80+87+98+108), leaving Title the arithmetic remainder 719−469 = 250. There is zero slack anywhere to move: 1px off Status breaks “In progress”, 1px off Updated splits a date, 1px off Assignee splits a handle, 1px off Severity wraps the header.

critique.good: Title at 291 is genuinely comfortable — long titles break at more natural clause boundaries and the column reads as the dominant one.
critique.problems: “In progress” splits into “In” / “progress”, and every date splits at the hyphen into “2024-” / “06-02”. Because the two most-scanned triage columns are now ragged, vertical comparison of status and recency collapses; every row becomes 60px and the table grows to 394px with no gain in information.
critique.cause: Status was cut to 82 (61px of text vs the 77px “In progress” needs) and Updated to 83 (62px vs the 87px a date needs) to fund the +41px title gain. The width was taken from the two columns whose whole value is being scannable in a straight line.

critique.good: The right rail is calm: Severity, Assignee, Status and Updated all single-line with visible air, and dates/statuses align perfectly for scanning.
critique.problems: The title is starved: long titles take three lines, row 3 jumps to 83px, and “long-running” is broken at its own hyphen, splitting a compound word. Meanwhile Status (112) and Updated (138) carry roughly 30–50px of dead space each, so the eye is drawn to empty metadata while the meaningful column is squeezed.
critique.cause: Over-allocation to Status (+14) and Updated (+30) beyond what their content needs, taken straight out of Title (206 = 185px of text, below the ~227px a 52-character title needs to stay at two lines).

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

ref_auto.why: ID breaks into “BUG-” / “2041,” dates split after “2024-06-,” and “In progress” wraps. Width is spent on secondary columns while atomic identifiers and dates are broken.

r0B.why: ID and title stay readable, but dates break after the year and “In progress” wraps. Secondary columns are over-wide relative to the cramped date/status fields.

ref_equal.why: The title is crushed into four or five short lines while other columns sit mostly empty. The primary scanning column is sacrificed, making rows very tall and comparison slow.

r0A.why: Title gets the dominant width and wraps only at natural spaces; ID, severity, assignee, status and dates stay intact on one line. Clear hierarchy and efficient row rhythm.

raw.unsure: Exact pixel widths are hard to measure from the renders, but the visible wrapping clearly distinguishes D from the others.

r0A.why: All six columns read cleanly: IDs, statuses and ISO dates stay on one line, while Title absorbs wrapping in two lines. Rows remain compact and scannable, with the wide descriptive column properly prioritised.

ref_equal.why: Title is starved while the other columns carry excess white space; titles break into four to six short lines, making rows very tall and cross-row comparison slow. The core descriptive column no longer reads as a phrase.

ref_auto.why: ID and Updated dates break at hyphens ('BUG-'/'2041', '2024-06-'/'02'), and Status splits 'In progress'. Identifiers and dates lose their integrity, which undermines scanning despite a reasonable Title width.

r0B.why: ID and Title remain intact, but Status wraps and every Updated date splits after '2024-', weakening the date column's scanability and producing uneven row heights. Better than C, but less clean than A.

raw.unsure: Whether wrapped ISO dates should be treated as disqualifying or merely suboptimal; exact column widths cannot be measured precisely from the images.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
